sentences.text: Sarcosaurus woodi is the sole known species within the extinct genus, whose name translates from Greek as "flesh lizard" or "meat lizard".
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — belonged to a bipedal predator measuring 3.5 meters in length and weighing no more than 50 to 60 kilograms.
A referred specimen, cataloged as NHMUK PV R3542, represented a larger individual estimated to reach 5 meters in length and weigh 140 kilograms.
A theropod tibia discovered in Northern Ireland stands as one of the very few dinosaur remains known from the island, which possesses a notably poor Mesozoic fossil record.
Confusingly, Friedrich von Huene named the same 445-millimeter tibia both Sarcosaurus andrewsi and Magnosaurus woodwardi in a single publication.
Charles William Andrews formally described the type species in 1921 after S.L. Wood discovered a partial skeleton near Barrow-on-Soar.
This partial skeleton was recovered from the Lower Lias formations of Leicestershire and Warwickshire.
Additional fossils were unearthed between 1980 and 2000 on a beach near The Gobbins in Northern Ireland by paleontologist Roger Byrne.
In 2020, a comprehensive new description proposed that three distinct specimens actually belonged to the same species, Sarcosaurus woodi.
Sarcosaurus was a bipedal predator capable of running fast to catch small prey.
The parent group of Sarcosaurus is the superfamily Coelophysoidea.
Andrews originally assigned the genus to the family Megalosauridae, but later analyses placed it in Ceratosauria or Coelophysoidea.
In 2018, Andrea Cau identified Sarcosaurus as a dilophosaurid with strong data support in a major analysis.
By 2020, Ezcurra et al. classified Sarcosaurus as a close relative of Averostra based on shared skeletal characters.
Sarcosaurus lived in what is now Europe, specifically England, Ireland, and Scotland, during the Early Jurassic, approximately 199 to 196 million years ago.
The time range for the genus spans from the Hettangian to the Sinemurian, roughly 201.4 to 192.9 million years ago.
Fossils were found in strata deposited in shallow, marine settings with a warm and humid climate, including the Rugby limestone member at a paleolatitude of approximately 35° N.

It is debated whether the two named species of Sarcosaurus are distinct, with some authors considering them indistinguishable and others labeling them as nomina dubia due to a lack of unique features.
